description:
Save $50 on a comma four (and support the channel) using my referral code: https://refer.comma.ai/PM65UJR

Today we’re revisiting the Tesla vs Openpilot comparisons with a REAL follow-up test. Last time we compared Tesla’s Enhanced Autopilot to Comma.ai’s Openpilot with Sunnypilot running on my Rivian R1T—and Openpilot won 26.5 to 21.5 using our 6-category scoring system.

This time we’re testing Tesla FSD v14.2.1 to see how much progress Tesla has made and how it stacks up. We took my wife’s 2023 Model Y on a similar route and graded FSD with and without a destination entered into navigation.

Has FSD improved enough to catch up—or even pass—Openpilot? Join us to see how it scores and compares!

Chapters
0:00 Intro
1:21 Testing FSD without a destination
3:49 FSD has a mind of its own
8:07 Handling curves very nicely
8:39 FSD fails a left turn
11:04 I want to make an exit, FSD has other plans
15:30 We enter a destination into navigation
16:49 Smoothly getting onto the highway
18:08 Discussing FSD curbing our wheels
21:21 Arriving and parking at our destination
22:42 Ali takes the driver's seat on the way home
27:41 Recording our scores
28:37 We discuss our experience
41:10 Final scores revealed

#fsd #autopilot #openpilot #tesla #commaai #handsfree

comments.text: I use OpenPilot/BluePilot on other vehicles, and would happily move or add one of those units to a Tesla vs paying a perpetual subscription for a feature on my car. comments.text: @theelectricvalentines I only say pointless because FSD is on a whole different level. Comma is more of a comparison for Tesla auto pilot because they do the same thing which is lane centering and some slight curves.
comments.author: @Murphys_Law9

comments.text: ​ @Murphys_Law9  Comma does more than lane centering and slight curve. It's handling 90+ degree turns on my Rivian, has hands-free anywhere (Autopilot doesn't have hands-free at all), and runs experimental mode (traffic light and stop sign recognition) with develipment on large-models using the recently released eGPU. That puts it somewhere between Autopilot and FSD, not a straight Autopilot comparison. Definitely agree it's very car-dependent though.

comments.text:
As someone who has worked with Openpilot for years (check my channel if you don’t believe me), I think that Openpilot is hands-down, the best *assistant* that exists on the market today. 

Back in 2021 when we were looking for ways to make it better, a few of us came up with the idea for split ACC/LKAS. That’s when Jason Wen (the founder of sunnypilot) reached out and took that concept and built upon it with a whole fork full of custom features. That’s what Openpilot is all about… customization.

That being said, I also have a HW4 Tesla Model 3. It’s hard to compare FSD because, if I was in the back seat of the car, I’d want FSD any day of the week. They just need to solve the speed limit and model desire noise (lane change twitches). 

However, being in the driver’s seat with FSD right now has made me feel embarrassed as a driver with some of the awkward movements and indecision it’s been making. This is why I believe a fully fledged system such as Openpilot really bridges that gap without trying to go full-out autonomous. But it’s very hard to compare because they are two completely different systems with different goals in mind.

comments.text: Tesla's Full Self-Driving (Supervised) v14.2.1 is not designed to be used without a destination. It fundamentally relies on a navigation route to provide context for path planning, lane changes, turns, and arrival behaviors like parking. The official release notes for software version 2025.38.9.6 (which includes FSD 14.2.1) describe its core functionality as: "Under your supervision, Full Self-Driving (Supervised) can drive your Tesla almost anywhere. It will start from a parked position, make lane changes, select forks to follow your navigation route, navigate around other vehicles and objects, make left and right turns and park at your destination." Without entering a destination, there's no defined route for the system to follow, which would limit it to basic behaviors like staying in a lane or following traffic flow—similar to earlier Autopilot features, not the advanced end-to-end autonomy of FSD.

I would love for non-destination signalling, but it kind of defeats the purpose of the goal of autonomy if the user is doing all the lane selection and decision making.
